blocks.prompt: The First Teachers
blocks.text: Here is something strange. The word school comes from an old Greek word. That word meant free time. In Greece, long ago, only people with spare time could sit and learn. Now school is for everyone. The very first teachers we know about lived in a place called Sumer. That was more than four thousand years ago. Their school was called a tablet house. The kids did not have paper. They wrote on soft clay with a sharp reed. Some of those clay tablets are still here. You can see a kid's spelling mistakes from four thousand years ago.

blocks.prompt: One Teacher, Eight Grades, One Room
blocks.text: In 1913 there were about two hundred thousand one-room schools in the United States. One room. One teacher. Every kid in the neighborhood, from the six-year-olds to the fourteen-year-olds, all on the same benches at the same time. Think about what that teacher had to do. She taught reading to the little ones while the older ones worked on math in silence. Then she switched. She hauled in wood for the stove. She swept the floor. She was often only sixteen or seventeen years old herself. Kids wrote on slates, which are thin sheets of dark stone in a wooden frame. Paper cost too much to waste on practice. You wrote, the teacher checked it, you wiped it clean, and you wrote again. Then came the blackboard. A teacher in Scotland named James Pillans is often given credit for it, around 1801. He wanted to draw big maps his whole class could see at once. That was the trick: one teacher, one surface, thirty kids all looking at the same thing. Almost every classroom in the world copied it. Today fewer than two hundred one-room schools are left.

4.title: The Teacher Who Waits Three Seconds

meta.templateLabel: The Teacher Who Waits Three Seconds

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Mary Budd Rowe timed classroom pauses in the 1970s
The average wait after a question: about one second
Three seconds of silence made answers longer
Socrates wrote nothing down
Sensei is Japanese for born before
Doctor comes from docere, Latin for to teach

blocks.prompt: The Silence After the Question
blocks.text: A teacher asks a question. The room goes quiet. How long does that quiet last? In the 1970s a researcher named Mary Budd Rowe decided to actually measure it. She recorded hundreds of classrooms and timed the gap between the end of a teacher's question and whatever happened next. The average was about one second. One second, and then the teacher would rephrase the question, or call on the fastest hand, or simply answer it themselves. Rowe then asked teachers to try something uncomfortable. Wait three seconds. Just three. Say nothing. The results were not small. Students gave longer answers. More students volunteered. They started backing up their answers with reasons instead of guesses. They asked more questions of their own. Kids who almost never spoke began to speak. Nothing about the students had changed. The only thing that changed was the silence. This is one of the oldest ideas in teaching, dressed up in data. Socrates, two and a half thousand years ago, taught almost entirely by asking. He wrote nothing down. He would ask a question, listen to the answer, and ask a better question about the answer. His students did the thinking. He did the asking. A good teacher is not a person who knows the most. A good teacher is a person who knows what to ask, and can stand the quiet afterward.

answers: the gap between a teacher's question and what happened next; the average was about one second
answers got longer, more students volunteered, answers had reasons instead of guesses, students asked more of their own questions
(inference: some kids need longer to turn a thought into words, so the fastest hands always win)
(inference: he believed understanding has to be built by the learner, not handed over)

blocks.prompt: Why the Person Who Knows It Is the Worst Person to Explain It
blocks.text: In 1990, a Stanford graduate student named Elizabeth Newton ran an experiment so simple it barely looks like one. She split people into pairs. One person, the tapper, got a list of famous songs and had to tap out the rhythm of one on a table. The other person, the listener, had to name the song. Before the listener guessed, Newton asked the tapper to predict the odds. Tappers thought listeners would get it about half the time. The listeners got it 2.5 percent of the time. Three out of one hundred and twenty. The tappers were not fools. They were stuck. Inside a tapper's head, the song is playing in full: melody, words, drums, everything. What the listener receives is a series of dull knocks on a table. The tapper cannot unhear the music, and so cannot imagine what the knocking sounds like from the other side. Psychologists call this the curse of knowledge. Once you know a thing, you lose the ability to remember not knowing it. And this is the central problem of teaching. The moment you become an expert, you become worse at explaining, because the gaps that confuse a beginner have closed up in your own mind and become invisible to you. This is why the smartest person in the room is so often the least useful explainer, and why a kid who learned fractions last week can sometimes teach them better than a mathematician. There is a strange flip side. Researchers have found that when students are told they will have to teach the material to someone else, they learn it better, even if the teaching never actually happens. Just expecting to teach changes how you read. You stop skimming. You start hunting for the main point, organizing it, looking for the sentence that would make it click for another person. Teaching is not what you do after learning. Teaching is one of the ways learning happens. So the next time an adult explains something and you do not follow, consider that the failure may not be yours. They may simply be tapping.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Teacher Who Waits Three Seconds

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Skhole: the Greek root of school meant leisure
Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve in 1885
Newton's tapping study, 1990: tappers guessed 50 percent, listeners scored 2.5
Rowe, 1972: average wait after a question was about one second
Pedagogue: Greek for the person who walked a child to school
Sensei means born before; guru means the weighty one

blocks.prompt: The Curse of Knowing: What Actually Makes Someone a Teacher
blocks.text: Ask most people what makes a great teacher and you will hear some version of the same answer: they really knew their subject. It is a reasonable guess. It is also, as far as the research goes, close to the least useful thing you can say about teaching. Consider what an expert's mind actually looks like. In 1990, a Stanford researcher named Elizabeth Newton had one person tap the rhythm of a well-known song on a table while a partner tried to name it. Tappers predicted their partners would succeed about half the time. The real figure was 2.5 percent: three correct guesses out of one hundred and twenty. The tappers were not overconfident so much as trapped. Inside their heads the song was playing in full, orchestrated and obvious. Outside, there was only knocking. Psychologists named the effect the curse of knowledge, and it describes the exact predicament of every expert who has ever stood in front of a confused room. Knowledge does not merely fail to make you a good explainer. It actively erodes your memory of what confusion feels like, and confusion is the thing you are being paid to navigate. So if not knowledge, what? Start with an inconvenient finding from 1885. Hermann Ebbinghaus, working alone and using himself as his only subject, memorized long lists of nonsense syllables and then tested how quickly he lost them. The curve he plotted falls off a cliff. Most of what he learned was gone within days. Forgetting is not a malfunction of learning. Forgetting is the default state, and everything a teacher does is a fight against that slope. The tools that actually win that fight are unglamorous and slightly unpleasant. Rereading a chapter feels productive and does almost nothing; closing the book and forcing yourself to recall what was in it feels awful and works. Cramming the night before produces a grade and no memory; the same hours spread across three weeks produce a memory and, usually, a better grade. Good teachers do not hand students information. They engineer the conditions in which students have to retrieve it, repeatedly, uncomfortably, until it stops slipping away. Then there is the smallest skill of all. In the early 1970s, Mary Budd Rowe listened to hundreds of recorded classrooms and timed the pause after a teacher asked a question. The average was roughly one second. Then the teacher rephrased, or called on the quickest hand, or answered it herself. Rowe asked teachers to hold the silence for three seconds instead. Answers got longer. More students volunteered. Students began offering evidence rather than guesses. Children who had been written off as slow turned out to have been merely slower than one second. The students had not changed. The teacher had learned to shut up. This is the pattern underneath all of it. Teaching looks like transmission, one full head pouring into thirty empty ones, and it is not. It is closer to construction work carried out by the student, in which the teacher's job is to keep asking, keep waiting, keep making the student do the hard retrieval, and to remember, against every instinct, what it was like not to know. Which raises an uncomfortable question about the phrase we all use. We say a teacher taught us something, as though the teaching were the thing that landed. Ebbinghaus, Newton and Rowe all point elsewhere. The teacher tapped. The learning was ours.
